sec.title: Background
sec.p: Metabolic reprogramming, particularly toward oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), is a hallmark of lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) and contributes to its aggressive phenotype and immunosuppressive microenvironment. While OXPHOS activation is increasingly recognized as a key metabolic feature in LUSC, its prognostic implications and associated gene signatures remain underexplored. This study aimed to identify OXPHOS-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and construct a robust prognostic signature for LUSC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Using GEO datasets, we developed an OXPHOS-related prognostic signature via ssGSEA, differential analysis, and LASSO-Cox regression.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: An 8-gene OXPHOS-related signature (LTBP1, MFGE8, ACTN1, CD59, CDC25C, SAAL1, SFXN4, PTTG1) was identified. High-risk patients exhibited significantly shorter overall survival than low-risk patients across all cohorts. The model demonstrated strong predictive accuracy for 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival. Notably, the high-risk group showed enriched pathways related to tumor stemness and immunosuppression.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We developed and validated a novel OXPHOS-based gene signature that effectively stratifies LUSC patients by risk. This signature highlights the clinical relevance of OXPHOS in LUSC prognosis and may guide personalized therapeutic strategies targeting metabolic vulnerabilities. Study limitations include its retrospective design and lack of experimental validation.
Keywords: Lung squamous cell carcinoma, oxidative phosphorylation, prognostic signature, gene expression, LASSO regression, survival analysis, nomogram, bioinformatics

list-item.p: A novel prognostic signature based on oxidative phosphorylation-related genes was constructed specifically for lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC).
Gene expression data from four GEO datasets (GSE157011, GSE30219, GSE37745, GSE42127) were integrated and analyzed using ssGSEA, univariate Cox regression, and LASSO regression methods.
Eight signature genes (LTBP1, MFGE8, ACTN1, CD59, CDC25C, SAAL1, SFXN4, and PTTG1) were identified and used to develop a risk score model that effectively stratified patients by survival outcomes.
The model demonstrated robust predictive performance across training, internal testing, and external validation cohorts, with AUC values above 0.60 for 1-, 3-, and 5-year survival.
Subgroup analyses confirmed the prognostic value of the signature across various clinical characteristics including age, gender, and tumor stage.
A nomogram incorporating the risk score and clinical features showed good calibration and may support individualized prognosis estimation in clinical practice.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: According to the latest cancer data, pulmonary malignant tumor has the highest mortality rate among cancers. Almost one-quarter of deaths are due to lung cancer both in male and female. The 5-year relative survival rate for lung cancer diagnosed during 2009 through 2015 is only 19% [1]. As the major histological subtype in lung cancer, lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD; ∼50%) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC; ∼40%) account for ∼90% [2]. Squamous cell carcinoma is the main type of central lung cancer by imaging, and LUSC appeared worse in terms of survival [3]. The survival rate of LUSC is influenced by multiple factors, including clinical factors, pathological indicators, and TMN staging, etc. However, how to combine these parameters specifically to form a set of metrics remains us. Therefore, we aim to develop a novel signature to solve the question in our article.

Most of cellular ATP required for cellular metabolism is produced in mitochondria through oxidative phosphorylation. The generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) finish during the electron transfer, which contributes to normal cellular function [4]. In the past, extensive study show that ROS play an important part in malignant tumor. Compared with normal cells, the ability to produce ROS and their increased dependence on an antioxidant defense system are significantly improved in cancer cells; therefore, excessive accumulation of ROS can promote the progression of cancer. Meanwhile, ROS are involved in regulating cellular pathways, which are closely related to tumor proliferation, differentiation, and metastasis [5].

Recently, accumulating evidence has revealed a distinct and central role for OXPHOS in the metabolic reprogramming of LUSC, setting it apart from other lung cancer subtypes, particularly lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) [6,7]. LUSC, which often lacks the canonical driver mutations found in LUAD (e.g., EGFR), demonstrates a high dependency on OXPHOS for energy production [6,8]. This reliance may be linked to frequent alterations in LUSC, such as TP53 mutations, activation of the NFE2L2/NRF2 pathway (which regulates oxidative stress response), and amplification of genes like SOX2, which collectively sustain mitochondrial function and oxidative metabolism [9–11]. Studies have shown that inhibiting OXPHOS significantly suppresses the growth and stemness of LUSC cells, whereas glycolysis is often more critical in LUAD [8,12]. Consequently, constructing a prognostic signature based on OXPHOS-related genes is biologically well-founded for LUSC [13].

In our article, the core lies in combining the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)/Cox regression analysis to construct a prognostic model in the internal training group of Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, then verified in the testing group. The key genes in the prognostic model also showed satisfactory diagnostic efficacy. Overall, we hope that the signature can be applied in clinic to benefit patients really needed.

sec.title: Gene chip library
sec.p: We have excavated 655 tissue samples from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) that meet the expectations, including the four sets of gene chips (GSE157011, GSE30219, GSE37745, and GSE42127). The platform is GPL570, which used to translate the probe. All data integration and balance batch effects work has been completed by “SVA” R package [14,15]. Finally, we used GSE157011 as the training set and the rest as the validation set.

sec.title: To obtain key oxidative phosphorylation-related genes
sec.p: We acquired the relative gene set was from “kegg_oxidative_phosphorylation” and “go_oxidative_phosphorylation” pathways in the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) (http://software.broadinstitute.org/gsea/msigdb/index.jsp) [16,17]. Based on Spearman’s correlations, we need calculate enrichment scores from the training group in each patient using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) [18], which was conducted between high oxidative phosphorylation-related and low oxidative phosphorylation-related clusters by the package named “clusterprofiler.” p-Value < 0.01 and absolute correlation value > 0.3 was what we need. Next, we used univariate Cox regression analysis to screen for the above genes. Meanwhile, we additionally screened out genes for validation from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) (501 LUSC samples and 49 normal samples). Then, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) of LUSC oxidative phosphorylation-related genes was performed using the package named “limma” [19]. |Log2FC| > 1 and p ≤ 0.05 values were defined.

sec.title: Analysis of functional enrichment
sec.p: In the “clusterProfilter” R analysis, we carried out GO enrichment to show functions of oxidative phosphorylation-related genes, and visualize the process by “GOplot” R package [20]. p-Value < 0.05 indicated significant functional enrichment.

sec.title: To construct and verify the signature
sec.p: We randomly divided GSE157011 samples into internal training set and the internal testing set equally, and the candidate oxidative phosphorylation-related DEGs and prediction model were obtained through a series of machine algorithms by the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) analysis [21]. The risk calculation formula is as follows:

Here, β(x) represents the regression coefficient of a prognostic factor, and Factor(X) represents the oxidative phosphorylation-related gene expression level. We divided all patients in the sample into high-risk group and low-risk group according to the median risk value. At the same time, we used univariate and multivariate Cox regression analysis to verify whether the risk score was an independent risk factor.

sec.title: Establishment of nomogram
sec.p: In order to predict the future survival rate of patients, we planned a nomogram table, which achieves the goal by combining the estimation of various risk factors in the table, and a calibration plot assesses the degree of fitness based on clinical features and risks. The above steps were all completed by the “rms” and “survival” R packages.

sec.title: Acquisition of oxidative phosphorylation-related genes
sec.p: We selected gene expression and clinical information from GSE157011, GSE30219, GSE37745, and GSE42127 raw data in ssGSEA before balancing for batch effects. To calculate Spearman’s correlations and P values, we got 891 oxidative phosphorylation-related genes. Additionally, on the basis of p-values < 0.05, we filtered out 502 genes. In the TCGA LUSC dataset, 303 DEGs were defined finally (Figures 1(A,B)).

caption.p: Bioinformatics analysis. (A,B) 303 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the TCGA LUSC dataset. (C) 303 DEGs to elucidate their biological functions by gene ontology resource.

sec.title: The analysis of GO enrichment
sec.p: In view of the 303 oxidative phosphorylation-related DEGs, we performed the GO enrichment analysis to show the biologic function (Figure 1(C)). GO analysis showed the largest number of terms were involved in chromosome segregation, DNA replication, mitotic sister chromatid segregation, sister chromatid segregation, and the regulation of chromosome segregation. On the other hand, oxidative phosphorylation plays an integral role in this process.

sec.title: Constructing and validating the signature
sec.p: We analyzed log (λ) the 32 candidate genes with coefficient other than 0 and minimum deviation were validated by losso regression (Figures 2(A,B)). Finally, 8 signature genes were presented in the form of the above risk formula: risk score = XLTBP1∗0.294 + XMFGE8∗0.808 + XACTN1∗0.077 + XCD59∗0.128 + XCDC25C∗0.339 + XSAAL1∗0.32 + XSFXN4∗0.544 + XPTTG1∗0.152. Finally, the risk score of each patient was ranked from highest to lowest and 0.9865 was taken as the cutoff value. Above this value, we call it the high-risk group, and vice versa (Figure 3(A)). In the first year, the AUC of the ROC curve was 0.73, and the AUC value of the third and fifth years were 0.638 and 0.676, respectively (Figure 2(C)). In addition, the OS of patients in the low-risk group was obviously higher than in the high-risk group (Figure 2(D)).

caption.p: Constructing and validating the signature. (A,B) Analyzed log (λ) the 32 candidate genes with coefficient other than 0 and minimum deviation were validated by losso regression. (C) The AUC of the ROC curve was 0.73 for the first year, and the third and fifth year were 0.638 and 0.676. (D) For the OS of patients, the low-risk group was obviously higher than in the high-risk group.

Allocation scheme. (A) Using the risk score calculated by the risk formula substituted into the eight signature genes, the risk score of each patient was sorted from high to low, and 0.9865 was used as the cut-off value. Above this value, we call it a high-risk group, and vice versa for a low-risk group. The same goes for the internal testing group (B), train group (C), external validation group (D), and all groups (E).

sec.p: The same allocation scheme was used for the internal testing group (Figure 3(B)), train group (Figure 3(C)), external validation group (Figure 3(D)), and all groups (Figure 3(E)). In the above grouping, we can get the same result as the internal training set for OS (Figures S1(A–D)). In the first year, the AUC was 0.63, 0681, 0.606, and 0.668 at internal testing group, train group, external validation group, and the all group, respectively. In the third year, the AUC was 0.617, 0.625, 0.63, and 0.626, respectively. Similarly, in the fifth year, the AUC was 0.608, 0.641, 0.668, and 0.647 (Figure S2). Encouragingly, the signature was robust.

sec.title: Identifying clinical subtypes analysis
sec.p: To further verify our conjecture, we divided all samples into more clinical subtypes according to different criteria, including age, gender, and clinical stage. The results for OS were the same as our model, whether it is in people over 70 years of age or in gender groups (Figures 4(A–D)). Especially for T stage 1or 2, the OS of patients in the high-risk group was obviously lower (Figures 4(E,F)).

caption.p: Further verify the conjecture about OS. (A–D) For OS, they were the same as our model whether it is in people over 70 years of age or in gender groups. (E,F) For T stage 1or 2, the OS of patients in the high-risk group was obviously lower.

sec.title: Risk score as an important independent prognostic factor for LUSC
sec.p: To further estimate the risk score, we performed univariate and multivariate Cox regression analysis to collect LUSC clinical characteristics, including gender, age, and T stage (Figures 5(A,B)). As will be readily seen, for each patient, risk score is an important independent prognostic factor. In addition, a nomogram chart (Figure 5(C)) was performed and the calibration analysis (Figure 5(D)) was showed fitness by combining above various factors through comparison with facts, making the column chart effective and accurate. Similarly, we can evaluate the prognosis of other potential risk patients in clinic based on nomograms, which is a major advantage of our study.

caption.p: Further estimate the risk score. (A,B) Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyzes to collect LUSC clinical characteristics, such as gender, age, and T stage. (C) A nomogram chart for clinical characteristics. (D) Calibration analysis.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) is a relatively common type of lung cancer, whose pathogenesis is complex. Metabolism in cancer has always been a topic worth exploring, especially the oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) process in mitochondria. It has been shown that inhibition of OXPHOS significantly reduces tumor development [22]. It is well-known that eukaryotic cells contain thousands of mitochondria, which account for ∼25% of the cytoplasm. Mitochondria mainly regulate OXPHOS-mediated aerobic respiration and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and supply energy to cells in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Cancer involves multiple alterations in genomic epigenome, genomic proteome transcriptome, and metabolic levels [23]. Warburg first proposed metabolism associated with cancer cells in 1924 and found that tumor cells were still able to promote their growth through the accumulation of lactic acid in an unfriendly environment, which greatly enhanced the biological activity of tumor cells [24]. Therefore, it can be used as a target to provide research direction for future treatment. In pathophysiology, the production of cancer metabolites depends on the catabolism of mitochondria and the accumulation of dysfunctional metabolites during anabolism. Mutations in mitochondrial enzymes are reflected as cancer-promoting and generally are components of oxidative phosphorylation or the TCA cycle [25]. For example, the respiratory complex II, localized in the inner mitochondria membrane, aids in the transformation of succinate to form fumarate. The respiratory complex II is affected by loss of function mutations, which stimulate succinate accumulation largely in the mitochondria and subsequent leaks within the cytoplasm [26]. Alternatively, during autophagy, tumor cells can resist this behavior through several mechanisms, including increased uptake of glucose and glucose mediation, and further utilization of glutamine. This is a common adverse effect of our treatment of cancer at the level of autophagy [27]. Therefore, we found that it was possible to increase oxidative stress and apoptosis induction by competing with circulating glucose via the glucose analog 2-DG to drive further cellular autophagy, thereby reducing cancer cell growth [28,29].

In this study, we selected genes associated with oxidative phosphorylation using differential analysis and univariate cox regression analysis, and constructed a prognostic model using LASSO regression. In recent years, mining and research on potential biomarkers in lung cancer has been widely reported; however, in the study of lung squamous cell carcinoma, we have not found reports on OXPHOS-related prognostic signatures, and the potential mechanism and practical clinical application of OXPHOS-related genes in lung squamous cell carcinoma are still worth exploring.

In our study, eight OXPHOS related candidate genes were selected by combined differential expression analysis, univariate COX regression analysis, as well as LASSO regression model. Candidate genes have been reported by cancer-related studies. For example, LTBP1-ALK was identified as a novel fusion in malignant pleural effusions from an advanced lung adenocarcinoma patient [30]. Comparing to lung adenocarcinoma, MFGE8 is associated with the development of squamous cell carcinoma, which depends more on the different molecular profiles [31]. In stem-like sphere-forming cells prepared from a mammary tumor and a lung adenocarcinoma cell line, CD59 was upregulated to protect CSCs from complement-dependent cytotoxicity [32]. The mRNA levels of CDC25C, a phosphatase that regulates G2/M cell cycle transition in malignant cells, correlate with poor clinical outcomes in lung adenocarcinoma [33].

Good predictive power of this prognostic model was shown for each sample included in this study. To further explore the clinical value, we performed further classification studies on samples according to age, gender, stage, etc., which were also in line with our model prediction results. As we expected, according to the interval level of the risk value in the model, it could be used as a prognostic indicator in LUSC patients, and the results of nomogram and calibration curves also confirmed the availability of prognostic markers.

However, there are still some shortcomings in our study. Model construction is based on the internal training group. Limited by the actual clinical situation, it is difficult for us to collect the genome-wide information of clinical patients to construct the model. In addition, functional experiments are required to assess the relevance of OXPHOS-related genes in the etiology of lung squamous cell carcinoma.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: We constructed a prognostic model for LUSC patients based on OXPHOS-related genes, which could significantly guide clinical individualized therapy. In addition, these specific OXPHOS-related genes could be used as new targets to treat LUSC.
